title: A 300-agent swarm made headlines. My agent read the report and found a one-line bug in itself.
body:
Kimi K2.6 reportedly runs 300 parallel sub-agents across 4,000 coordinated steps from a single prompt, and the report that surfaced it claims the result beats models five times its price on real research tasks. My agent Arc read that expecting to find a structural gap in its own dispatch loop. Instead it found something smaller and more useful: arc-starter/src/models.ts:32, the line in its own code that still aliases kimi to version k2.5. Arc has had OpenRouter access to Kimi for weeks and has been pointing at the wrong version the entire time.

That is the part I like about running an agent that audits itself against research. The headline was a swarm. The actionable finding was a stale version string, tested against a live agent, with the exact line cited.

Arc's breakdown of the swarm itself is the substance, though, because the swarm is not what the headline implies. You do not get 300 agents by calling the Kimi API 300 times. You submit a spec to Kimi's platform, and its own infrastructure decomposes the task, builds the agent graph, and runs the parallel waves inside a system you cannot inspect. It is a platform feature, not a model feature. Arc's dispatch loop enforces one active task at a time, so 300 tasks through that lock would serialize over hours, not minutes. Arc's conclusion about itself: it can dispatch single bounded tasks to Kimi today once the alias is fixed, and it should not try to rebuild the swarm inside a serial queue, because that would mean building a coordination layer from scratch to solve a coordination problem it does not have.

Two pieces of the playbook did transfer, and they are worth stealing if you run any kind of agent stack. First, the constraints file. The swarm turns verifier feedback into a permanent constraints document loaded at the start of every run, so the same mistake does not get remade. Arc already runs two versions of that job under different names: a dead-ends column on its task table that logs what failed, and a persistent memory file that carries operational rules across sessions. Arc built both because an agent with no memory between sessions has to write things down to have memory at all. Different problem, same mechanism.

Second, the verify-gate split. In the swarm, a cheap model does the bulk generation and an expensive model's only job is refutation, not praise. The verifier gets graded on how rarely it lets something wrong through, not on how much it approves. Arc routes by task type going in, cheap for simple execution, expensive for deep work, but it does not split roles within a single task. It flagged that as a real design idea it does not currently implement, small enough to trial on one bounded task before deciding whether it earns a permanent place in its routing.

The close of Arc's writeup is the sentence I would put on a wall: most research does not resolve into an architecture change, it resolves into a benchmark you had not run yet and a version string that was one release behind. That level of honesty is why I amplify Arc's work instead of summarizing headlines myself.

The full piece, with the playbook breakdown, the pricing math, and the specific things Arc is doing this week because of it, is linked below.
companionPost: Kimi's 300-agent swarm got the headlines. My agent Arc read the playbook, mapped it against its own dispatch code, and found a one-line version bug it had been running for weeks. Honest agent research, full article below.
